14437-historical-view-of-the-languages-a:
Talvi, the pen name of Therese Albertine Luise von Jakob Robinson, published this 1850 New York survey of Slavic languages and literatures, with a preface by Edward Robinson. It was among the first English works to treat the field as a whole.

Chapters trace Russian, Polish, Czech, Serbian, Croatian, Bulgarian, and smaller Slavic tongues, their histories, alphabets, and early printed books. A closing sketch samples popular poetry, including songs and ballads. The book opened Slavic letters to American readers, and its breadth still impresses, even where later scholarship has corrected it. Its author wrote under a pen name drawn from her initials.
20921-adventures-in-the-arts-informal-ch:
True artists refuse to shelve life in one snug, fixed idea, argues Adventures in the Arts. Most folk, it says, lock life away young in a tidy mental box. Marsden Hartley's informal chapters on painters, vaudeville, and poets push back hard.

Hartley, a noted American painter, writes of art with a maker's frank eye. Studios, stages, circuses, and poems all feed his roving talk. He prizes fresh seeing over stock taste at every turn. The book gives readers a vivid, quirky tour of creative life in the 1920s, told by a man who lived it from inside.
22523-the-history-of-the-american-expedi:
Joel R. Moore, Harry H. Mead, and Lewis E. Jahns wrote the history of the American expedition fighting the Bolsheviki. American troops served in Russia after the First World War. Their own unit history opens with America's war declaration.

Congress declared a state of war with Imperial Germany, the document begins. That declaration set the chain of service in motion for these men. From training camps they shipped to a very different front. In north Russia they fought Bolshevik forces around Archangel. Cold, confusion, and an unclear mission marked that campaign. The veterans' history preserves orders, rosters, and memories in detail. It remains a key record of America's forgotten Russian intervention.
23971-the-best-of-the-world-s-classics-r:
Henry Cabot Lodge and Francis W. Halsey edited The Best of the World's Classics, Restricted to Prose, in ten volumes, and this sixth volume covers Great Britain and Ireland, part four, from 1801 to 1909. Funk and Wagnalls published it in 1909, with Ruskin, Dickens, Thackeray, and Darwin on the frontispiece.

Contents include John Henry Newman on Tractarianism and his submission to the Catholic Church, Bulwer Lytton on the descent of Vesuvius upon Pompeii, and Lord Beaconsfield's Jerusalem by moonlight. Merivale on Augustus Caesar and Kinglake on mocking follow. With introductions and biographical notes, the volume is a portable anthology of nineteenth-century British prose at its best.
24693-william-black-the-apostle-of-metho:
John Maclean wrote this life of William Black, apostle of Methodism in the Maritime Provinces of Canada, published at Halifax in 1907. Maclean notes that earlier sketches all rest on the Memoirs of William Black by Matthew Richey, published at Halifax, and his own book builds on that foundation.

Chapters follow Black as a maritime itinerant, riding and preaching through Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, to his last days and after. Maclean, author of Canadian Savage Folk, writes with respect for a pioneer preacher. Readers of Canadian church history will find here a compact life of a remarkable evangelist.
28026-great-pianists-on-piano-playing-st:
James Francis Cooke published Great Pianists on Piano Playing in Philadelphia with Theo. Presser Company in 1913, subtitled study talks with foremost virtuosos. The book presents personal educational conferences with renowned masters on technic, interpretation, style, and expression.

Twenty-one chapters interview artists from Pepito Arriola and Wilhelm Backhaus to Ferruccio Busoni, Teresa Carreño, Josef Hofmann, Rachmaninoff, and Sauer, on topics from the artist's life to learning a new piece. The volume remains a lively source for piano students on how great players thought about their art. Cooke opens with a father asking a famous educator whether his talented, healthy, ambitious daughter can become one of America's greatest pianists.
28058-a-text-book-of-precious-stones-for:
Frank B. Wade, head of chemistry at Shortridge High School in Indianapolis, published A Text-Book of Precious Stones for Jewelers and the Gem-Loving Public with G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1918, reprinted in 1924. Wade, author of Diamonds, writes twenty-nine lessons on distinguishing stones, refraction, hardness, dispersion, and color.

Later lessons treat naming, sources, cutting, forms, imitations, color alteration, and pearls, including cultured pearls. Illustrated and practical, the book taught jewelers and buyers how to judge gems by science rather than by eye alone, and it remains a useful introduction to gemology.
30051-the-history-of-woman-suffrage-volu:
Ida Husted Harper edits the sixth and final volume of The History of Woman Suffrage, covering 1900 to 1920 and published in 1922 by the National American Woman Suffrage Association. State-by-state accounts record the long push for the vote, while the frontispiece shows Carrie Chapman Catt riding from a New York station after Tennessee completed ratification of the Federal Suffrage Amendment. Forty years of effort, traced in the prior volume, reach their end here.

Catt led both the International Woman Suffrage Alliance from its founding in 1904 and the national association in two terms. Copperplate and photogravure portraits fill the volume, and its chapters give organizers, campaigns, and setbacks their due. For students of American reform, the book is the capstone record of how the vote was won, state by state and vote by vote.
7338-studies-in-the-life-of-the-christia:
Henry T. Sell's Studies in the Life of the Christian asks what Christ taught, what the standpoint of Christianity is, and what a Christian is. It asks what he ought to believe and why, and how he should regard the Bible and the church. Relations to God, fellow men, home, society, business, and state follow, with the strength and reasonableness of the great main positions of faith and service set out constructively.

Careful attention goes to applying Christian principles to the perplexing problems of modern life, and Sell wrote the book for adult Bible classes and study groups. His tone is plain, practical, and pastoral rather than polemical. Readers get a manual for belief lived out in daily duty.
7561-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-l:
Two memoirists speak for the courts of Louis XV and Louis XVI in this volume of short passages and pictures: Madame du Hausset and the Princesse de Lamballe. Both women lived inside the old regime's inner rooms. Their notes catch rank, money, and intrigue as daily business. Each passage can be traced to its full scene, so court talk stays tied to its moment.

Read together, the passages sketch a world near its end, still polished and still scheming. Clerical wealth, party canvassing, and the power of rank recur across them, alongside sharp notes on flattery and folly. The value lies in the viewpoint: women close to power, watching it closely. It is a compact guide to the last years of the old regime, told from within.
8358-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-58-colo:
Colossians is a short letter to a small church in Asia Minor, warning it against teachers who mixed philosophy, angel worship, and strict rules with the gospel. Paul, or a writer in his name, answers with a hymn to Christ as the image of the unseen God, firstborn of creation, in whom all things hold together. The letter then turns practical: put off anger and lying, put on kindness and patience.

Household rules and a note about a letter to Laodicea close the book. In Challoner's Douay-Rheims wording, the argument keeps its older Catholic tone. Colossians matters for its high view of Christ, and for showing how early churches guarded a simple message against fashionable additions.
8373-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-73-apoc:
Apocalypse is the Douay-Rheims name for Revelation, the last book of the Bible. John, exiled on Patmos, writes to seven churches in Asia Minor in visions. Seals break, trumpets blow, a beast rises from the sea, and Babylon, the great city, falls in a single hour. The book closes with a new heaven and earth, and a city whose gates never shut.

Challoner's revision from the Vulgate keeps the older title and the book's wild imagery. First readers, living under Rome, likely read it as coded resistance: empires fall, God wins, and the martyrs are vindicated. Later readers have matched its beasts to every age's tyrants. Either way, it ends Scripture not with argument but with a vision of home.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-vi:
Tome six of the French al-Masudi came from Barbier de Meynard's hand in 1871. Les Prairies d'Or renders the Muruj al-Dhahab, the great tenth-century summa of the Baghdad traveler al-Masudi. The Société Asiatique printed the nine tomes between 1861 and 1877, with Pavet de Courteille sharing the labor.

The work treats the world whole. Its seas and rivers, its peoples and their kings, its faiths and its wonders all pass in review. The history of Islam follows, year by year. Al-Masudi reports marvels with a traveler's shrug and hard facts with a scholar's care. In French the book became Europe's fullest door into his mind. This tome is the sixth stretch of the road.
britannica-1911-john-v-or-vi:
John V or VI (1332–1391), surnamed Palaeologus, was East Roman emperor and the son of Andronicus III, whom he succeeded in 1341. At first he shared power with his father's friend John Cantacuzene. After a quarrel between them, Cantacuzene in practice displaced him for a number of years, from 1347 to 1355.

His reign saw the slow break-up of imperial power. His own son Andronicus rebelled against him, and the Ottomans pressed ever harder on what was left of the empire. He made a vain bid for papal help by submitting to the supremacy of the Roman Church. In 1381 he owned himself a tributary of the Ottomans. The short entry rests on those bare facts: a child accession, a shared and lost throne, revolt inside the family, and slow surrender to a stronger neighbour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-vi: Boniface VI held the papacy for only fifteen days in 896, and his election was later declared null. A Roman chosen in a popular tumult after Formosus, he had twice been deprived of his orders, as subdeacon and as priest. The Council of Rome under John IX in 898 pronounced his election void. Some say he died of gout, while others say he was forced out to make way for Stephen VI, the Spoletan party's candidate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ercole-consal:
Ercole Consalvi was a cardinal and statesman, born in Rome on 8 June 1757 and dead there on 24 January 1824. His ancestors belonged to the noble Brunacci family of Pisa, one of whom settled at Toscanella in the Papal States about the middle of the seventeenth century. His grandfather Gregorio Brunacci inherited a large fortune from Ercole Consalvi of Rome on condition of taking the Consalvi name and arms.

At nine, Ercole was placed in the college of the Scolopii at Urbino, where he stayed from 1766 to 1771. From 1771 to 1776 he was in the seminary of Frascati, finishing rhetoric, philosophy, and theology, and gaining the protection of the Cardinal Duke of York. From 1776 to 1782 he studied jurisprudence and ecclesiastical history in the Academia Ecclesiastica of Rome, where the Jesuit scholar Zaccaria was among his professors. He then entered public life, named private chamberlain by Pius VI in April 1783.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-vi:
Henry VI, German king and Roman emperor, was born in 1165 as son of Frederick Barbarossa and died in 1197. Pale and solitary where his father had been imposing, he was nonetheless great in conception and energy, pursuing his aims with a restlessness that often made him seem hard. His ambition aimed at world empire, its key Sicily, claimed through his wife Constance, daughter of Roger II.

Crowned emperor at St. Peter's in 1191, Henry's first Sicilian expedition failed amid rebellion stirred by Henry the Lion's escape and the murder of Albert of Liège. Fortune turned when Richard of England, captured on his return from Palestine, fell into Henry's hands, paralysing princely opposition. His second expedition of 1194 entered Palermo without opposition. The birth of his son Frederick the next day gave tangible shape to his dream of an hereditary imperial crown uniting Sicily with the empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mondovi:
Mondovi is a Piedmontese diocese in the province of Cuneo, northern Italy. Its city rises on three hills some 1,600 feet above sea level and dates from the year 1000. Its suburb of Breo recalls a Roman-era colony. The town, once under the bishops of Asti, broke free as a commune in 1198.

Freedom brought long struggle. Mondovi fought the bishops of Asti, the marquesses of Saluzzo and Monferrato, and the counts of Savoy. It shifted allegiance from lord to lord until it settled under Savoy in 1418. French and imperial armies later contested it. The entry follows the diocese through its bishops, churches and parishes into modern times.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-jean-o:
Pierre Jean Olivi was a thirteenth-century Franciscan thinker whose strict reading of his order's rule of poverty set him against his own superiors. He was born at Sérignan around 1248 and joined the Friars Minor as a boy. He studied at Paris and became the leading voice of the rigorists, friars who wanted the rule kept in its hardest form.

Chapters of the order accused him of heresy and seized his writings in 1283. They censured dozens of his claims, though later chapters partly cleared him. He taught at Florence and Montpellier before dying at Narbonne in 1298. Even after death the fight went on, as friends honoured his tomb like a saint's while the Council of Vienne in 1312 ruled against three of his teachings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-v:
Pope Adrian VI reigned from 9 January 1522 to 14 September 1523, the last non-Italian pope of his era except Marcellus II to keep his baptismal name. He was born of humble parentage at Utrecht on 2 March 1459 and lost his father early. His widowed mother's fortitude kept him at school. He studied first at home, then at Zwolle with the Brothers of the Common Life, and finally at Louvain. There he became Doctor of Divinity in 1491.

As professor of theology at Louvain he wrote a commentary on Peter Lombard's Sentences and quaestiones quodlibeticae. In 1506 Maximilian chose him as tutor to the young Charles V. Within a decade he rose to bishop of Tortosa, Grand Inquisitor of Spain, cardinal, and regent of Spain, before the Sacred College's unanimous call to Rome surprised him as much as anyone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-alexande:
Pope Alexander VI, born Rodrigo Borgia at Xàtiva near Valencia on 1 January 1431, ruled from 1492 to 1503 and stands as the Renaissance's most notorious pope. Jofre Lançol fathered him, and his mother Isabella Borja was sister to Cardinal Alfonso Borja, afterwards Callixtus III. His uncle's rise in 1455 fed his ambition, and adoption into the Borja house left him known as Borgia.

Cardinal-deacon from 1456 at twenty-five, he ran the Roman Church's vice-chancellorship from 1457 with uncommon prudence and skill, yet piled up archbishoprics, bishoprics, and abbacies like Leporello's catalogue. Pius II scolded him in 1460 over scandalous behaviour at Siena. Ordained priest in 1468, he kept to his wicked courses. Still, his good looks, easy manner, and sparkling talk charmed his age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict VI, birth date unknown, died in August 974. A Roman, son of Hildebrand and Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Theodore, he succeeded John XIII, dead 6 September 972. Waiting for Emperor Otto's approval held his consecration back until 19 January 973. Of his acts almost nothing survives, beyond confirming privileges for certain churches and monasteries.

His pontificate's most dramatic moment is its grim ending. A noble faction under Crescentius and the Deacon Boniface VII seized him and cast him into Castel Sant'Angelo. There, confined under two months, he was strangled on their command, lest Sicco, Otto II's envoy to Rome, secure his freedom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement VI, born Pierre Roger in 1291 at Maumont in Corrèze, was elected at Avignon on 7 May 1342 and died there on 6 December 1352. At ten he entered the Benedictine monastery of La Chaise-Dieu, studied at Paris, and became doctor and professor there. Introduced to John XXII, he rose swiftly. He became prior of Saint-Baudile and Abbot of Fécamp. He was Bishop of Arras and Chancellor of France in 1328, Archbishop of Sens in 1329, of Rouen in 1330, and cardinal in 1338.

His policy showed excessive devotion to France and his kin, hampering his mediation between England and France, though it won a short truce at Malestroit in 1343. Most of his twenty-five cardinals were French, twelve his relatives. He bought Avignon's sovereignty for 80,000 florins from Joanna of Naples in 1348. He confirmed Cola di Rienzi's ephemeral Roman rule in 1347 and granted the jubilee every fifty years instead of a hundred.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory VI, born John Gratian, was elected on 1 May 1045, abdicated at Sutri on 20 December 1046, and died probably at Cologne early in 1048. In 1045 the youthful libertine Benedict IX held Peter's chair. Anxious, it is said, to marry, he asked his godfather Gratian, Archpriest of Saint John at the Latin Gate and a man of great uprightness, whether he might resign.

Convinced he might, Benedict offered the papacy to his godfather for a sum, and Gratian, in good faith and simplicity, paid it and was recognised as pope. His accession, hailed even by Saint Peter Damian, brought no peace. Sylvester III, set up by the faction that had driven Benedict out in 1044, still claimed the chair, and Benedict himself repented and claimed it again. Aided by his chaplain Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII, Gregory strove by letters, councils, and arms to restore order, but the antipopes' factions proved too strong.

Pope Gregory XVI, born Bartolomeo Alberto Cappellari at Belluno on 8 September 1765, reigned from 1831 to 1846 as a Camaldolese monk-pope and defender of papal authority. Of nobility, he entered San Michele di Murano as a novice in 1783, taking the name Mauro, was professed three years later, and ordained in 1787. He taught philosophy and theology to juniors and became censor of books for his order and the Venetian Holy Office in 1790.

In 1799, the year Pius VI died in exile at Valence after Berthier's abduction, Dom Mauro published The Triumph of the Holy See, upholding papal infallibility and temporal sovereignty. It drew little notice until he became pope, then reached three editions and translations. Under Pius VII he became abbot of San Gregorio in 1805 and procurator general in 1807. After Napoleonic expulsions and the closure of San Michele, he taught at Murano and Padua before his rise to the cardinalate and the papacy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent VI, born Etienne Aubert at Mont in the Diocese of Limoges, was elected at Avignon on 18 December 1352 and died there on 12 September 1362. He began as professor of civil law at Toulouse, rising to its highest judicial position. Entering the Church, he became Bishop of Noyon in 1338, of Clermont in 1340, cardinal-priest in 1342, then Ostia's Cardinal-Bishop and Grand Penitentiary in 1352.

The conclave that elected him framed the first certain election capitulation, each cardinal binding himself to divide power and revenues with the College. Aubert accepted the engagement only where it squared with church law. Once chosen, one of his first acts declared the pact illegal and null, as limiting the divinely conferred papal power. He ordered Avignon's place-seeking clergy back to their residences under pain of excommunication, repealed some of his predecessor's benefice appointments, abolished reservations, and disapproved pluralities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-vi:
Pope John VI, a Greek whose birth date is unknown, reigned from 701 to 705 and died on 11 January 705. He ascended the throne on 30 October 701. During his reign Theophylactus, chamberlain, patricius, and exarch of Italy, came to Rome from Sicily. Suspecting his visit boded no good, local militias marched to Rome and encamped outside the walls, showing their dislike of the exarch.

To avoid bloodshed, John sent priests to them and succeeded in pacifying them, at least as far as the exarch himself was concerned. Before disbanding, the militias insisted that certain informers, whose denunciations had put citizens' wealth into officials' hands, be handed over for punishment. Taking advantage of discord between exarch and Italians, the Lombards renewed attacks, seizing towns of the Duchy of Rome. With no one able to resist by arms, John sent priests with money to Duke Gisulf's camp, ransoming all captives and persuading him to retire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xv-:
Pope John XV, enthroned in 985, dead in April 996, shares one entry with John XVI. Boniface VII the usurper died in July 985 after eleven months in power. John, a Roman, son of the presbyter Leo, then won election and coronation sometime between 6 August and 5 September 985. A handful of later chroniclers and papal lists name a second John, Robert's son, as Boniface's heir, with a supposed four-month reign.

That phantom pope never lived, yet his listing scrambled the Johns' numbering, so the real John XV often passes as John XVI. Meanwhile the patrician John Crescentius, Duke Crescentius's son, gripped Rome's temporal power. Some chroniclers say his dominance so galled the pope that John fled to Tuscany seeking Empress Theophano's help. Crescentius even barred access to the pope without bribes, yet his pledges lured John back to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-vi:
Leo VI was a Roman and the son of Christopher. His father had been a leading official under John VIII. Leo served as cardinal-priest of St Susanna. He became pope in the second half of 928. The dates of his election and death stay uncertain. A reign of seven months and five days would place his death in February 929.

His main surviving act settled church jurisdiction in Dalmatia. A bull gave Archbishop John of Spalato the pallium. That woollen band marked his rank. The bull ordered Dalmatian bishops to obey him. It confined Bishop Gregory to Scodra. Tradition adds only that most writers say he was buried in St Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-vi:
Giovanni Angelico Braschi was born at Cesena in 1717 to a noble but poor family. He studied at the Jesuit college there and law at Ferrara. After a Naples mission he took posts as papal secretary and St Peter's canon in 1755. Clement XIII made him treasurer in 1766, and Clement XIV made him cardinal in 1775. Spain, Portugal, and France first opposed his election, thinking him a friend of the Jesuits.

He let Jesuits keep schools in Prussia and continue in Russia. He travelled to Vienna in 1782 to face Joseph II, who barred bishops from appealing to Rome and shut monasteries. The emperor received him with respect, but his minister slighted him. Later, Naples left thirty sees vacant in 1784 and sixty by 1798 over royal nominations. In 1788 his bull erected the see of Baltimore for the United States. He died at Valence in France in August 1799.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-:
Stephen reigned from 885 to 891 and died in September 891. His father Hadrian gave his schooling to Bishop Zachary, the Holy See's librarian. Marinus I made Stephen cardinal-priest of SS Quattro Coronati. His obvious holiness won him the papacy. His September 885 consecration came without waiting for imperial confirmation, but Charles the Fat let it stand given the election's unanimity.

Famine from drought and locusts met an empty treasury, so Stephen spent his father's wealth relieving the poor, redeeming captives, and repairing churches. Guido III of Spoleto became his adopted son and won the emperor's crown from him in 891. When Lyons's archbishop refused to consecrate the duly elected Teutbold of Langres, Stephen consecrated him himself. He resisted Bordeaux, Ravenna, and Photius's attacks on Rome, and his resistance succeeded. He begged the emperor for warships and soldiers against Saracen assaults. He was buried in St Peter's portico.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-vi:
Bartolomeo Prignano was born at Naples about 1318 and died at Rome on 15 October 1389. He went young to Avignon and won powerful friends. He became archbishop of Acerenza in 1364 and of Bari in 1377. While the vice-chancellor stayed at Avignon, Prignano ran the papal chancery. After Gregory XI died, the 1378 conclave weighed him for his business skill, integrity, and legal knowledge.

The conclave of 7 April held four Italians, five French, and seven of the Limoges faction. Italians and French, each pushing their own men, agreed to block a Limoges candidate and chose a prelate outside the College. Robert of Geneva and Pedro de Luna both yielded their claims for Prignano. But the French cardinals soon protested fidelity while meeting to void the April election, and won over the Italians. Their August Declaration attacked Urban passionately, and they left Anagni for Fondi under his enemy's protection. The Western Schism had begun.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-vi:
Raymond the Sixth, Count of Toulouse, was born in 1156, died in 1222, and succeeded his father Raymond the Fifth in 1195. This encyclopedia entry paints a debauched and sceptical prince, who put away three wives in turn and took as his fourth Jeanne, sister of Richard the Lionheart. Loaded with the Church's benefits, he treated the heretical Cathares, or Albigenses, with the greatest kindness, though his father had persecuted them. He refused to molest them, let them preach before him, and perhaps joined their sect.

His court was dissolute, and he ignored the reproof of Innocent the Third's legate, Pierre de Castelnau, who excommunicated him in 1207. Shortly after, an equerry of the count treasonably killed Castelnau, and the pope deposed Raymond at once. Frightened into submission, Raymond expelled the heretics from his lands. Later he retook Toulouse in November 1217, holding it against Simon de Montfort, who was killed in June 1218.
doe-osti-1774872-american-made-challenge:
Sound-based cleaving of gallium arsenide is the subject of National Laboratory of the Rockies report NREL/TP-5900-79624, issued in February 2026 with Emily Warren as technical contact. The report closes out CRADA project CRD-19-00831. The work supported the Department of Energy's American-Made Challenges Solar Prize. It sized up Sonic Wafering, a method that uses sound to cleave thin layers from gallium arsenide, a costly high-efficiency solar material, so the parent wafer can be reused.

Prize funds were shifted from analysis work to hands-on demonstration, and the planned analysis task was dropped before the project began. The laboratory's tasks centered on growing test structures in several rounds. One structure checked the accuracy of the cleaving itself. A second, a double heterostructure, tested surface treatments called passivation. Samples were measured before and after new passivation layers, and cleaved pieces were processed into working devices such as solar cells.
doe-osti-2997296-realizing-the-materials:
Ryan Alberdi, Craig Hamel, Aabhas Singh, and co-authors rethink how printed structures are designed for the places they will serve, in Sandia report SAND2025-11989R dated September 2025. Additive manufacturing can vary material inside a part, but standard design tools assume one material picked in advance. The project instead optimizes shape and material together, under realistic nonlinear mechanics.

Methods include a robust search for stable mechanical balance in soft metamaterials, materials built from repeating cells that bend and stretch by design. Math tools keep the design field well behaved by penalizing drift from a true signed distance field. Differentiable simulations let the optimizer follow gradients through the physics. The payoff sought is parts designed for their actual loading environment from the first sketch, rather than adapted afterward.
doe-osti-2997456-high-power-fpc-progress:
Brookhaven National Laboratory technical note BNL-229012-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-144, by Wencan Xu, J. C. Brutus, Z. Conway, and co-authors, tracks progress on the power coupler for the Electron-Ion Collider's electron ring cavities. A fundamental power coupler is the armored waveguide that pours radio power into a superconducting cavity. This design handles 400 kilowatts continuously.

Design choices include a thick 10.5 millimeter radio window, a long gap from window to choke tip so the brazed joint can be inspected, and a coaxial line tuned for lower field and fewer multipacting zones. Cooling runs 5 kelvin helium at 200 milligrams per second, holding heat leak to the 2 kelvin bath at 4.2 watts. The titanium nitride coating on the window measured 10 plus or minus 5 nanometers nearly everywhere, within the stated tolerance. High-power testing is expected to start in mid-2026.
doe-osti-3004275-radioisotope-science-an:
Hunter Andrews and sixteen colleagues compile a division yearbook in Oak Ridge report ORNL/SPR-2025/4240, dated September 2025. It summarizes fiscal 2025 core research in the Radioisotope Science and Technology Division. Oak Ridge is the nation's main source of many medical and industrial radioisotopes. The report covers competitive internal projects, postdoctoral researchers, and student interns in one volume.

Project summaries run from new measurement tools to production methods. One featured effort improves bismuth targets for making astatine-211, a promising cancer therapy isotope: electrodeposition studies at the University of Washington, then examination at Oak Ridge after irradiation. The division uses the volume to show sponsors the year's spread of work and to give early-career researchers a citable record of their projects.
doe-osti-3008860-optimize-the-autonomous:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory CRADA final report number 476, by Daniel Deng, Aljon Salalila, Jun Lu, Jayson Martinez, and Hongfei Hou, dated November 2024, closes work on optimizing the Autonomous Sensor Fish. The Sensor Fish is a small instrumented device released through dams and turbines to record what a real fish would endure.

Much of the report inventories the project's output: conference abstracts and presentations from 2021 to 2024. Entries cover in-situ hydraulic measurements in the lower Mekong River, metrics for predicting fish survival from sensor data, and combined sensor-and-simulation assessments of turbine passage. The record documents a device aimed at fish-friendly hydropower guidelines for marine and hydrokinetic systems as well as conventional dams.
doe-osti-3021636-development-of-high-thr:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report by Ernesto S. Nakayasu, Soumyadeep Sarkar, and Lye Meng Markillie, dated December 2025, develops faster laboratory assays for RNA modifications. Chemical marks added to RNA molecules after they are built change what the RNA does, and one such mark, ADP-ribosylation, is added by PARP-family enzymes. Measuring these marks has been slow and low-throughput, limiting both basic research and drug screening.

The team designed in vitro assays around PARP12, mapping its structure from a crystallography-determined catalytic domain and AlphaFold predictions of its remaining domains. Zinc finger domains that can grip DNA or RNA were part of the targeting picture. Using insulin messenger RNA as a test substrate, the assays detect its ADP-ribosylation with plate-reader chemistry suited to screening many samples at once. The methods aim at modification enzymes as future drug targets.
doe-osti-3021932-effect-of-the-form-of-c:
Vitreous State Laboratory final report VSL-18R4370-1, by Keith S. Matlack, Hao Gan, Malabika Chaudhuri, and co-authors of The Catholic University of America, examines how the chemical form of chromium affects Hanford high-level waste vitrification. Published in October 2024 and released under HFO-73191, the work matters because chromium limits how much waste a melter can take: in the wrong form it promotes crystals that clog glass production.

The team prepared blended waste simulants, including an SY-101/SY-102 blend, with chromium introduced in different forms, such as chromium oxide. Glass-forming additives were batched by weight to produce 100-kilogram-scale target glasses. Comparing the melts shows how chromium's starting form carries through to glass behavior. The findings feed the formulation rules for the Hanford Tank Waste Treatment and Immobilization Plant, where feed chemistry must be controlled before it reaches the melter.
doe-osti-3375617-extending-component-lif:
A final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-EE0009826 closes ECLAIIR, an Electric Power Research Institute project on solar inverter life. Wayne Li led the team, with Rabin Dhakal as certifying engineer. The project ran from March 2022 to November 2025. Inverters are the weak link in many solar plants. They fail years before the panels do, and each failure costs a truck roll plus lost output.

Much of the report is teardown notes on field-worn units, logged by serial number. One inverter held a piece of grass and no faults at all. Another showed ants inside as foreign contamination. A third had severe water ingress, with mineral stains throughout and melted insulation on its solar input cables. Eight of its ten cover screws were missing, which broke the gasket seal. Fixes are plain: covered spots, sound gaskets, thread locker on screws, and sealed cable entries.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CIAMarchettiVic:
Victor Marchetti had been a high-ranking CIA officer, a special assistant near the top of the agency, before he became its most troublesome defector in print. Penthouse magazine framed its interview with him as an open letter to the CIA.

Marchetti talks about covert operations, including the destabilization of Chile, from inside knowledge of the building he had served. His book The CIA and the Cult of Intelligence had already made legal history through the government's effort to censor it before publication. The interview is preserved as part of the seventies exposure wave, when former officers became the agency's loudest critics.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MertzMichaelVic:
An unnamed writer addressed this letter to 'Bud' on April 15, 1980. Its subject is what the writer calls the heroin angle. The letter discusses reporter Les Payne and 'The Heroin Trail,' a newspaper investigation of the drug trade. It also mentions the French SDECE, that country's foreign intelligence service. The author's name cannot be recovered from the garbled scan.

Heroin trafficking threads run through assassination research of the period, linking Marseille, intelligence services, and exile politics in researchers' theories. This letter shows one reader working those connections in private correspondence. It names its sources and its suspicions, even if the file cannot name the man who wrote it down.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-OgilvieClaytonC: nsia-OgilvieClaytonCorrespondence Ogilvie Clayton Correspondence: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, complete. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers.
historical-view-of-the-languages-and-lit:
Therese von Jacob, writing as Talvj, wrote this view of the Slavic nations' tongues and books. It came out at New York in 1850, with a preface by Edward Robinson. Talvj surveys language after language across the Slavic world. Dying tongues, like those of the Lusatian Wends, get full care.

The middle parts trace Czech, Slovak, and other letters in growth. Poets, playwrights, and translators of Shakespeare and Goethe are named. A fourth part sketches the popular poetry of the Slavs. For English readers of its day, the book opened a vast, little-known world of song and print.
nasa-tm-19640023414-mission-plan-tiros-v: The Aeronomy and Meteorology Division at Goddard Space Flight Center prepared this mission plan for the TIROS VI satellite. TIROS craft were America's early weather satellites, built to photograph clouds from orbit. A mission plan sets out a satellite's aims, orbit, and ground operations before flight. The hosted sample preserves only the plan's cover page, with no readable body text, so the plan's details cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19660007969-preliminary-results-:
Luther W Slifer Jr and Stephen G McCarron at Goddard reported early results in October 1965 from a solar cell test flown on Explorer XXVI. Different cell designs were mounted on the satellite. In orbit, radiation slowly damages solar cells and cuts their output. The experiment compares how well each design resisted that damage, the catalog note says.

Results are called preliminary, so the flight record was still short. Even early readings guide the choice of cells for later satellites. Power loss in orbit cannot be repaired after launch. A side-by-side test in real space was the surest way to learn which cell design aged most slowly.
nasa-tm-19700017984-space-manufacturing-:
Hans F. Wuenscher of the Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this report on July 11, 1969. It looks at kinds of manufacturing that only zero gravity makes possible. In orbit, melts and mixtures behave in ways they never do on Earth.

Without gravity, there is no sinking, rising, or settling in a cooling melt. Wuenscher surveys what could be made under those conditions. He treats factory work that the space setting itself enables, not work merely moved into space. Studies of this kind shaped early plans for space stations. They asked what products might one day justify building plants in orbit.
nasa-tm-19700026597-the-photoconductive-:
John J. Park of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this report in June 1970. It studies the light-sensitive layer inside AVCS-APT vidicon tubes. Vidicon tubes were the cameras that sent pictures from early weather and Earth-view satellites, so the quality of that layer set the quality of the pictures.

Park analyzes how selenium and sulfur amounts vary across layers on typical tube face plates. He also measures layer thickness and checks how the maker's own optical method skews those readings. Certain layers showed grain boundaries, a sign of an unacceptable light-sensitive coating. Electrical tests then trace how makeup and thickness changes affect performance, and point to a best thickness range.
peccavi: Hosted here, the sample shows only the front matter of Peccavi, the title pages, copyright page, and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names E. W. Hornung, author of The Amateur Cracksman, and the New York publishers Charles Scribner's Sons, 1901, with copyright dated 1900. The first contents entries are "Dust to Dust," "The Chief Mourner," "A Confession," and "Midsummer Night." The Latin title means: I have sinned.
podcast-joerogan-72P_9jmrOVI:
Ethnobotanist Dennis McKenna and Josh Wickerham join episode 477 of the Joe Rogan Experience. McKenna, brother of Terence, has studied plant medicines in the Amazon for decades. Wickerham works on sustainable sourcing of those same plants, and together they give the talk a field-work base.

They describe how Amazonian peoples use psychedelic plants in healing and ritual, and what science has confirmed so far. Rogan asks about the rush to commercialize these traditions and the harm it can do. The episode balances wonder with care, showing two experts who respect both the plants and the cultures that kept them.
podcast-joerogan-QHQzoHolWvI:
Comedian Theo Von joins Joe Rogan to tell how he tried ketamine therapy in a segment from the show. Von is a comic known for odd tales from a hard youth in the South. His drug tales mix pain with laughs.

Von tells what the clinic felt like, what the drug showed him, and what stuck when he came back. He weighs the help it gave his mood against the strangeness of the cure. Rogan asks the blunt bits his crowd wants to know. Listeners get a comic's frank take on a new cure. The library holds the segment as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-TyODZ4IjBVI:
Jason Silva, Duncan Trussell, and Ari Shaffir crowd into episode 369 of the Joe Rogan Experience, an early group session from the show's wild years. Silva is a futurist performer, Trussell the house mystic, and Shaffir a gleefully rude stand-up. Rogan hosts his friends like a party.

The talk spins through psychedelic tales and big ideas about tech and the mind, with Shaffir grounding every flight in a joke. No single subject owns the hour. The episode is a group portrait of Rogan's circle before fame sorted it, and a sample of the loose hang format the show grew from.
podcast-tuckercarlson-TSZXlVF-qVI:
Is there evidence of God in mathematics? Tucker Carlson takes up that question in a segment of his podcast. The claim is an old one in new dress: that the deep order of numbers, beautiful and unforced, points to a mind behind the world.

Carlson works through the argument with care, asking why math describes nature so well and whether chance can explain the fit. The talk speaks to his audience's wider interest in faith under pressure from a secular age. The segment is a short piece of popular theology, built on wonder at the strange fact that the universe can be read in numbers at all.
quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-louis-:
Quotes and Images from the Memoirs of Louis XV and XVI gathers extracts from two witnesses of the late French monarchy, Madame Hausset and the Princess Lamballe, arranged alphabetically by David Widger. Their courts were sliding toward revolution, and the lines catch both the polish and the rot.

A liar ought to have a good memory, one entry begins, and another notes a bad habit of talking indiscreetly before others. Beaumarchais sent arms to the Americans. The clergy held a third of the national revenues. A duchess can be made a beggar more easily than a beggar a duchess. Such sayings sketch a world under strain.
studies-in-the-life-of-the-christian-his:
Henry T. Sell wrote Studies in the Life of the Christian: His Faith and His Service as a study book matching his Bible studies on the lives of Christ and Paul. Sell, a doctor of divinity writing from Chicago, aims the book at adult Bible classes, study circles, pastors' training classes, and private study.

His preface lists the questions: what Christ taught, what a Christian is, what he ought to believe and why, and how he should regard the Bible and the church. Chapters treat Christ the great teacher, the Christian's God, the Christian man, his fellow man, faith, the Christian's book, and prayer. Sell promises a constructive statement with plain application to the problems of modern life.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-58-colossian:
Colossians, in the Douay-Rheims version, made from the Latin Vulgate and reworked by Bishop Richard Challoner between 1749 and 1752. Behind it stand a Rheims New Testament of 1582 and a Douay Old Testament of 1609 and 1610. An introduction says its doctrine is similar to what Paul set out in Ephesians.

Chapter one gives thanks for grace given to the Colossians and prays for them. Christ is named head of the church and peacemaker through his blood, with Paul as his minister. Paul writes as an apostle by God's will, with Timothy beside him. A church Paul did not plant receives a letter stressing Christ's fullness against teachings that would add lesser powers beside him.
the-bible-douay-rheims-book-73-apocalyps:
Apocalypse, in Douay-Rheims wording taken from the Latin Vulgate, with Bishop Richard Challoner's revisions of 1749 to 1752 applied. The New Testament portion traces to Rheims, 1582; the Old Testament portion to Douay, 1609 and 1610. Chapter one is headed as John ordered to write to seven churches in Asia, with a description of Christ appearing to him.

It opens as the Revelation of Jesus Christ, given to make known things that must shortly come to pass. God signified it by an angel to his servant John. A note debates the phrase the time is at hand. Visions, letters to churches, and warnings under persecution follow an opening that claims divine origin for every scene.
un-doc-united-nations-special-committee-:
Partition takes detailed shape in Chapter VI of the 1947 report of the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine. A majority of the panel backed splitting the mandate into two states, one Jewish and one Arab. Jerusalem was to sit under international rule, outside both states.

The chapter draws the proposed borders and explains the economic union that would still link the two states. It covers citizenship, holy places, and the steps for British withdrawal. Months later the General Assembly adopted a partition plan much like this one, and its lines still echo today.
